title: Streaming and latency
summary: Why AI answers appear word by word, how to stream them through your own server, and what to do when a job is too slow for one request.
youWillLearn: Why time to first token matters more to users than total time
How a streamed answer travels from the model, through your server, to the browser
Which timeouts sit in that chain, and who sets them
When to stop streaming and move work into a background job

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.Claude API: Anthropic's AI, reached over the internet: you send it text, it sends text back. Each call costs a little money.
glossary.token: A small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a word. Models read, write and bill in tokens.
glossary.latency: How long someone waits between asking and getting a result.
glossary.streaming: Sending a response in small pieces as it is produced, instead of all at once at the end.
glossary.time to first token: How long until the first piece of the answer arrives. It decides whether an app feels fast.
glossary.SSE: Server-sent events: a simple web standard where the server keeps one response open and pushes small text events down it.
glossary.timeout: A limit on how long something may run or wait. When it is hit, the work is cut off with an error.
glossary.background job: Work that runs outside the user's request, so the request can answer right away and the result arrives later.
glossary.worker: A separate program that picks up background jobs and runs them, with no user waiting on the other end.
glossary.polling: The browser asking again every few seconds: is it done yet?
glossary.abort: Cancelling a request that is still running, so neither side keeps working on it.

steps.title: Notely waits for the whole summary
body: Notely is our course's notes app. Maya clicks Summarize in her browser. The browser asks the app server (the computer running Notely's code), which asks the Claude API, Anthropic's AI.
The app server waits until the whole summary is written, then sends it back in one piece. For a short note, that takes about three seconds.

scene.caption: One click, one full answer, about three seconds.

steps.title: Twenty seconds of spinner
body: Maya summarizes a long note. A spinner turns for twenty seconds, then the whole summary pops in.

Nothing is broken. The model was writing the whole time, one token (a small piece of text) after another. Notely waited for the last one before showing anything. To Maya, that latency looks like a frozen app, so she clicks again.
changes: ~ First words 3 → 20 s
~ Request open 3 → 20 s
~ Browser: shows a spinner

scene.caption: The model writes for twenty seconds; Maya sees nothing until the end.

steps.title: Show the words as they are written
body: The fix is streaming: pass each piece along the moment it exists. The total time barely changes; what changes is the time to first token: Maya sees words within a second, and reading keeps pace with writing.
That is why AI chats type their answers out: it is the real speed of writing.

callout.text: A waiter who brings each dish as it is ready, instead of holding the whole order until dessert is done. The meal takes as long; nobody sits hungry.

changes: ~ First words 20 → 1 s
~ Browser: words appear as they are written
~ Small pieces flow back on every hop

scene.caption: Pieces of the answer flow back all the way to Maya as they are written.

steps.title: One response that stays open
body: With streaming on, the Claude API keeps one response open and pushes a series of small events down it. This web format is called SSE.

First a message_start, then many content_block_delta events with a few characters each, then message_stop. The SDK (Anthropic's helper library) turns these into simple callbacks, but you will see them in network logs.

code.caption: Shortened. Each event is a line of data pushed down the same open response.

changes: ~ Maya and Browser step back
~ Claude API: sends small events down one open response

scene.caption: Between the Claude API and the app server, one response stays open.

steps.title: Your server passes the stream along
body: The browser never talks to the model directly, because the API key must stay secret. So the app server relays: it opens a stream to the Claude API and returns its own stream to the browser.
On the page, code reads that response piece by piece and appends the text to the summary box.

code.caption: The server loads the note itself, by id, for the logged-in user. It never trusts note text sent by the browser.

changes: ~ Browser back in view
~ App Server: relays each piece to the browser
~ Claude API pill removed

scene.caption: The app server is a relay: pieces in from the model, pieces out to the browser.

steps.title: A chain of timeouts
body: Every hop has a timeout. The browser can give up, the host (Vercel) limits how long server code may run, and the SDK has its own limit.
The shortest one wins. Maya summarizes a whole notebook, and the app server is cut off while the model is still writing.

callout.text: On Vercel, a route can raise its own limit with export const maxDuration = 60 (seconds), up to what your plan allows. Check the current limits in the docs rather than an old blog post.

changes: ~ Request open 20 → 90 s: a whole notebook
~ App Server: cut off at its 60-second limit

scene.caption: The app server's time limit is the shortest in the chain, so it fails first.

steps.title: Too slow for a request: background it
body: Some jobs take minutes, too long to hold a request open. So the app server saves a background job in the database and answers at once with a job id.
A worker (a separate program) picks it up, calls the Claude API and saves the result. The page checks back by polling: is it done yet?

callout.text: You met queues and workers in system design. Same pattern here: the model call is the slow step the worker runs.

changes: + Database: keeps a jobs table with status and result
+ Worker: runs the job, no user waiting
~ Request open 90 → 0.2 s: the server answers at once
~ Maya steps back; the app server no longer calls Claude

scene.caption: The slow call moves to a worker. The request only creates the job.

steps.title: Notely: stream or background?
body: Ask one question: is a person watching and waiting for this exact answer?

Yes, within seconds: stream it (note summary, chat reply). No, or it takes minutes: background it (weekly digest email, importing 500 notes). Either way, save every result to the database so a refresh does not lose it.

callout.text: Ask: is streaming used for answers people watch? What is the route's maxDuration, and can the slowest case finish inside it? Is the finished text saved? For long jobs, what does the page show while it runs, or if it fails?

changes: − Maya, Browser, App Server, Claude API, Worker, Database
+ Note Summary and Chat Reply: someone waits, so stream
+ Weekly Digest and Bulk Import: minutes, so background

scene.caption: Four Notely features, sorted by one question: is someone waiting?

steps.title: Streams can break halfway
body: Once streaming starts, the app server has already said "success". If the API fails mid-answer, the error arrives inside the stream, so the page must handle it and offer a retry.
The opposite costs money: Maya closes the tab, but the server keeps reading tokens nobody sees. Pass the request's abort signal through, so the model stops too.

code.caption: When the browser goes away, cancel the call to the model.

changes: − Note Summary, Chat Reply, Weekly Digest, Bulk Import
+ Maya, Browser, App Server and Claude API: back to one stream
~ Browser: Maya closed the tab, the model keeps writing
~ Wasted tokens 0 → 900

scene.caption: Maya left, but the app server and the model keep working for no one.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Models write one token at a time. Streaming does not make that faster; it makes the first words arrive early.
Relay the stream through your own server, know the shortest timeout in the chain, abort when the user leaves, and save the final text. Jobs that take minutes run in the background.
changes: ~ Wasted tokens 900 → 0: the abort reaches the model
~ Every part back to a healthy, streaming state

scene.caption: First words in a second, nothing wasted.

quiz.question: A client says: "Streaming will make our AI answers finish faster, right?" What is the honest answer?

options.text: Yes, streaming uses a faster connection to the model.
options.why: The model writes at the same speed either way. Streaming changes when you see the text, not how fast it is written.

options.text: No. Total time is about the same, but the first words show up much sooner.
options.why: Streaming cuts time to first token. Users read as the model writes, so the app feels fast even when the full answer takes as long.

options.text: No, streaming makes answers slower because of the extra events.
options.why: The event overhead is tiny. The big effect is that users see progress almost immediately.

quiz.question: Notely's new "summarize all my notes" feature fails for heavy users with a timeout. What is the best fix?

options.text: Turn on streaming for that route.
options.why: Streaming still keeps the server code running until the last token. A job of several minutes still passes the host's limit.

options.text: Retry the request automatically until it works.
options.why: The job takes as long every time, so it will time out every time, and each retry costs tokens.

options.text: Return a job id right away and run the work in a background job.
options.why: Nobody is waiting on that exact second. A worker can take minutes, save the result, and the page picks it up when it is done.

quiz.question: Logs show many summaries that finish after users already left the page. What should Claude Code add?

options.text: A loading spinner so users stay on the page.
options.why: Users will always leave sometimes. The server still needs to stop work it no longer needs.
That lets answers grow longer, which makes the waste worse, not better.

options.text: Cancel the call to the model when the browser's request is aborted.
options.why: Passing the abort signal through stops the model from writing tokens nobody will read, which saves money.

takeaways: Streaming cuts time to first token. It does not make the model write faster.
The browser talks to your server, and your server relays the model's stream. The key never leaves the server.
Every hop has a timeout; the shortest one wins. Know your route's maxDuration.
Abort the model call when the user leaves, and save the final text to the database.
If a job takes minutes, return a job id and run it as a background job.
